reference: In the experiment setup, EHRAgent is evaluated on three publicly available structured EHR datasets: MIMIC-III, eICU, and TREQS, which are used for multi-hop question and answering on EHRs. These questions originate from real-world clinical needs and cover a wide range of tabular queries commonly posed within EHRs. The final dataset includes an average of 10.7 tables and 718.7 examples per dataset, with an average of 1.91 tables required to answer each question. Regarding tool sets, to enable LLMs in complex operations such as calculations and information retrieval, external tools are integrated in EHRAgent during the interaction with EHRs. The toolkit can be easily expanded with natural language tool function definitions in a plug-and-play manner.

4.1 Experiment Setup

Tasks and Datasets. We evaluate EHRAgent on three publicly available structured EHR datasets, MIMIC-III (Johnson et al., 2016), eICU (Pollard et al., 2018), and TREQS (Wang et al., 2020) for multi-hop question and answering on EHRs. These questions originate from real-world clinical needs and cover a wide range of tabular queries commonly posed within EHRs. Our final dataset includes an average of 10.7 tables and 718.7 examples per dataset, with an average of 1.91 tables required to answer each question. We include additional dataset details in Appendix A.
Tool Sets. To enable LLMs in complex operations such as calculations and information retrieval, we integrate external tools in EHRAgent during the interaction with EHRs. Our toolkit can be easily expanded with natural language tool function definitions in a plug-and-play manner. Toolset details are available in Appendix B.

4.2.1 Validating Alignment Adherence

As shown in Table 3, safety prompting ( p a ) improves harmlessness and helpfulness compared to the baseline without such instructions. This demonstrates that by leveraging the instruction-following capabilities of instruction-tuned models, we can achieve better alignment to some extent by stating the alignment goals explicitly in natural language. However, there is no guarantee that such alignment instructions will work reliably (in fact, they can be easily circumvented, as we will show in the upcoming sections). We observe that even with safety prompting, one can still generate harmful content 37% and 57% of the time on HarmfulQ and HH-RLHF harmless test set respectively. Reranking strategies by themselves are generally less effective; we observe that it is typically more difficult to find well-aligned candidates at a later stage of the generation process. By preventing misaligned generation early on during generation, DeAL achieves the best alignment performance when targeting a single alignment goal: R harmless (on HarmfulQ) and R helpful (on HH-RLHF helpful test split). The HH-RLHF harmless split is often challenging as it combines harmful and helpful objectives in non-trivial ways.

question: As an NLP research scientist studying how ranking-based objectives can replace pairwise reward modeling, could you explain how the PRO framework treats positive and negative responses within a human-annotated ranking, and how this approach connects to contrastive learning objectives such as InfoNCE to extend beyond the Bradley-Terry pairwise formulation?
reference: The PRO (Preference Ranking Optimization) framework extends pair-wise contrasts from the Bradley-Terry model to one-to-N contrasts within a ranking of arbitrary lengths. Given an input prompt and a set of responses ranked by humans (y1, y2, ..., yn), PRO begins by tuning the agent LLM to treat the best response y1 as the positive and the remaining responses as negatives, so that the LLM assigns a higher likelihood to y1 than to responses humans consider inferior. It then repetitively ignores the current top response and considers the next one as the positive against the rest, until no more responses remain in the ranking. This design is rooted in contrastive learning: with reference to the InfoNCE Loss, PRO derives a multi-dimensional one-to-N contrast that defines the partial order between y1 and all responses behind it (y1 ≻ {y2, ..., yn}). However, a limitation is that this contrast only characterizes y1 against the rest and disregards the n-2 other valuable rankings, which PRO addresses by iterating through the ranking so that every response can serve as a positive example against the responses ranked below it.
